description: Severity distribution for abrasion, friction, and surface contact injuries. Rubbing, scraping, rope burns, conveyor belt friction, grinding contact. Low-energy mechanical surface damage — distinct from struck (impact) and caught_in (entanglement/crush). Mostly non-SIF. P(death) scale from AIS mortality data.
assumptions: Surface friction/contact only — not entanglement in machinery (that's caught_in)
magnitude_note: Abrasion severity is limited by the energy transfer mechanism — friction removes surface tissue but doesn't transfer deep kinetic or thermal energy. The rare SIF pathway is secondary infection or friction contact with high-speed rotating surface (grinding wheel, belt sander) causing deep laceration.

magnitude_bands.description: Minor friction/rubbing injury. Rope burn, skin scrape against rough surface, manual handling abrasion, minor conveyor contact. Surface-level tissue damage only.
magnitude_bands.mortality_source: BLS nonfatal injury data: abrasion/friction injuries are high-frequency, low-severity. No fatality mechanism from surface abrasion alone.
magnitude_bands.rationale: Surface abrasion — skin removal, friction burns. Self-limiting because contact pressure is low. P90=first_aid reflects cleaning and dressing a graze. No SIF potential whatsoever.

magnitude_bands.description: Glancing contact with powered rotating surface. Grinder, belt sander, wire wheel, lathe workpiece. Brief contact producing deep abrasion or laceration but not entanglement.
magnitude_bands.mortality_source: OSHA machinery contact data: glancing contact with rotating tools produces deep lacerations but is distinct from entanglement (caught_in). Fatal only if contact is to neck/face with large grinding wheel.
magnitude_bands.rationale: Brief glancing contact with a powered surface produces deep abrasion or laceration. P90=medical_treatment reflects laceration needing sutures or skin graft. If the worker is drawn into the machine, the mechanism transitions to caught_in — abrasion covers only the surface contact without entanglement.

magnitude_bands.description: Sustained contact with high-speed surface. Dragged by conveyor belt, rope friction through hands (crane/winch), large grinding wheel contact. Higher energy transfer from speed and duration.
magnitude_bands.mortality_source: Conveyor belt injury data; industrial friction contact reports. Conveyor drag injuries can produce deep tissue damage and amputation but are usually survivable.
magnitude_bands.rationale: Sustained friction with a high-speed surface removes tissue deeply — degloving, deep burns, potential amputation. P90=serious_injury reflects extensive degloving or friction amputation. Crosses SIF threshold at P90 but only just. If the worker is pulled onto the conveyor, this transitions to caught_in.

surface_speed.description: Multiplier on P(death). Higher surface speed removes tissue faster and deeper.

sources.author: BLS
sources.relevance: Nonfatal injury survey — abrasion/friction is a high-frequency category. Nature code 13 (surface and flesh wounds).

sources.author: OSHA
sources.relevance: ITA Case Detail: contact with non-running objects (code 66) captures many abrasion events. 112,726 events in 2024.

sources.author: Baker et al.
sources.relevance: AIS mortality rates — foundation for P(death) scale

validation_notes: STKY check: rope burn should be NON_SIF — minor_friction P(SIF)=0.000 ✓
STKY check: conveyor belt drag should be ELEVATED — high_speed_friction P(SIF)=0.10 ✓

Cross-check: abrasion is fundamentally surface-level injury. The SIF pathway is almost always a mechanism transition — abrasion becomes caught_in (entanglement) or struck (if the grinding wheel shatters). The abrasion calibration should be low because if it escalates, the model should reclassify to the dominant mechanism.
